--- title: "Take-home Exercise 2" subtitle: "Local measures of spatial association and emerging hot spots of armed conflict in Myanmar, January 2021 to September 2025" author: "An Loc" date: "5 October 2026" date-modified: "last-modified" date-format: "D MMM YYYY" format: html: theme: light: cosmo dark: darkly css: ../../styles.css number-sections: true number-depth: 3 toc: true toc-depth: 4 toc-title: "On this page" toc-expand: true code-fold: false code-summary: "Show code" code-copy: true code-overflow: wrap code-line-numbers: false fig-align: center smooth-scroll: true grid: body-width: 820px margin-width: 345px gutter-width: 1.4rem fig-width: 7 fig-height: 5.5 knitr: opts_chunk: out.width: "100%" execute: echo: true eval: true warning: false message: false freeze: true --- # Introduction and study context {#sec-intro} On 1 February 2021 the Myanmar military removed the elected National League for Democracy government and formed the State Administration Council. Security forces killed more than six hundred protesters in the following months (Council on Foreign Relations, 2026). The first armed resistance by protesters was recorded in Kalay, Sagaing Region, on 28 March 2021. Armed resistance in Mindat, Chin State, began on 26 April 2021. The National Unity Government announced its People's Defence Force on 5 May 2021 (Wikipedia, "Myanmar conflict"). Before the coup, armed conflict in Myanmar was concentrated in the ethnic states along the land borders, where ethnic armed organisations have fought the military since independence in 1948 (Wikipedia, "Myanmar conflict"). Since the coup, fighting has been recorded in at least 321 of the country's 330 townships, including the Bamar-majority regions of central Myanmar, where little fighting was recorded in the decades before 2021 (Su Mon, 2024). More than 2,600 new non-state armed groups have been recorded since April 2021 (Su Mon, 2024). The newer groups use drones, improvised explosives and ambushes. The military uses airstrikes and ground assaults on villages (Su Mon, 2024). Ethnic self-determination, competition between armed groups over territory and resources, and opposition to the coup all drive the fighting, in different combinations in different areas (Su Mon, 2024; Wikipedia, "Myanmar conflict"). Armed conflict events are mapped here over the 57 months of the study period, to show where they concentrate, which townships differ from their neighbours, and how the spatial pattern changed. The 87,109 event records of the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED) for Myanmar, from 1 January 2021 to 30 September 2025, were aggregated to the 330 townships of the Myanmar Information Management Unit (MIMU) boundary layer, version 9.4. # Research questions and objectives {#sec-question} | Objective | Research question | Method | |--------------------|----------------------------------------------|----------------------------------| | Pinpoint hot spots, cold spots and spatial outliers of violence | **RQ1.** Which townships belong to clusters of high or low counts of armed conflict events, and which differ from their neighbours, at p < 0.05? | Local measures of spatial association: local Moran's I, local Geary's c, Getis-Ord Gi and Gi* (@sec-lmsa) | | Reveal where, how fast and in what pattern violence evolved | **RQ2.** Where did hot and cold spots of armed conflict events emerge, intensify, persist or fade between 2021 and 2025? | Emerging hot spot analysis on a space-time cube (@sec-ehsa) | RQ3 and RQ4 extend the objectives of the exercise: - **RQ3.** Do the three event types (battles; explosions and remote violence; violence against civilians) concentrate in the same townships? (@sec-lmsa-types) - **RQ4.** Did the local Moran's I clusters of armed conflict events change after the Operation 1027 offensive began on 27 October 2023? (@sec-value-added) # Data and study design {#sec-data} ## Software and packages ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} pacman::p_load(sf, sfdep, spdep, tmap, tidyverse, seastests, Kendall, modifiedmk, ggrepel, knitr, kableExtra, patchwork) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"} `p_load()` loads the packages and installs any that are missing: **sf** for the vector data, **sfdep** and **spdep** for neighbours, weights and the spatial statistics, **tmap** and **tidyverse** (ggplot2) for maps and charts, **seastests**, **Kendall** and **modifiedmk** for the seasonality and trend tests, and **knitr**, **kableExtra**, **ggrepel** and **patchwork** for tables, labels and layouts. ::: ## Sources | Dataset | Source | Content | Licence | |--------|------------------------------------------|----------------------------|---------------------| | ACLED events, Myanmar | ACLED, provided on eLearn | 87,109 events, 1 Jan 2021 to 30 Sep 2025, 31 fields | ACLED terms of use; kept out of the public repository | | Township boundaries | MIMU GeoNode, layer `mmr_polbnda_adm3_250k_mimu_1`, "Myanmar Township Boundaries MIMU v9.4" (18 Jun 2023) | 330 townships, EPSG:4326, digitised at 1:250,000 | Free with attribution | | Township population | OCHA, Common Operational Dataset on Population Statistics, `mmr_admpop_adm3_2023.csv` | Department of Population projection for 2023, based on the 2014 census | CC BY | ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} acled <- read_csv("data/aspatial/ACLED_Data_Myanmar_Jan2021-Sep2025.csv") |> mutate(event_date = as.Date(event_date)) tsp <- st_read("data/geospatial/mmr_polbnda_adm3_250k_mimu_1.shp", quiet = TRUE) |> st_transform(32647) |> arrange(TS_PCODE) pop <- read_csv("data/aspatial/mmr_admpop_adm3_2023.csv") |> select(TS_PCODE = ADM3_PCODE, pop = T_TL) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} # north arrow and scale bar for the ggplot maps, in the style of tm_compass() and tm_scalebar() gg_key <- function(x, y, u, km = 200, north = NULL, at = NULL) { add <- \(d) if (is.null(at)) d else cbind(d, at[rep(1, nrow(d)), , drop = FALSE]) bar <- add(data.frame(xmin = x, xmax = x + km * 1000, ymin = y, ymax = y + 0.012 * u)) lab <- add(data.frame(x = c(x, x + km * 1000), y = y - 0.022 * u, key_txt = c("0", paste(km, "km")))) out <- list( geom_rect(data = bar, aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax), fill = "white", colour = "black", linewidth = 0.4, inherit.aes = FALSE), geom_text(data = lab, aes(x, y, label = key_txt), size = 3, inherit.aes = FALSE)) if (!is.null(north)) { cx <- north[1]; by <- north[2]; ty <- by + 0.075 * u; hw <- 0.016 * u; ny <- by + 0.02 * u half <- \(sx) add(data.frame(x = c(cx, cx + sx * hw, cx), y = c(ty, by, ny))) out <- c(out, list( geom_polygon(data = half(-1), aes(x, y), fill = "white", colour = "black", linewidth = 0.4, inherit.aes = FALSE), geom_polygon(data = half(1), aes(x, y), fill = "black", colour = "black", linewidth = 0.4, inherit.aes = FALSE), geom_text(data = add(data.frame(x = cx, y = ty + 0.025 * u)), aes(x, y), label = "N", size = 3.4, inherit.aes = FALSE))) } out } ``` ::: ::: {.panel-tabset} #### Table ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} |layer | rows|crs | |:---------------|-----:|:-----------------------------------------| |ACLED events | 87109|WGS 84 coordinates in longitude, latitude | |Townships | 330|EPSG:32647 | |Population rows | 330|none | ::: ::: #### Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tibble(layer = c("ACLED events", "Townships", "Population rows"), rows = c(nrow(acled), nrow(tsp), nrow(pop)), crs = c("WGS 84 coordinates in longitude, latitude", st_crs(tsp)$input, "none")) |> kable() ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"} `read_csv()` and `st_read()` read the events and the township layer. `st_transform(32647)` projects the townships to UTM zone 47N, so that distances are in metres. `arrange(TS_PCODE)` sorts the townships, because `emerging_hotspot_analysis()` assigns its results by row order (@sec-ehsa). `select(TS_PCODE = ADM3_PCODE, pop = T_TL)` keeps two population columns under new names (`new_name = old_name`). Myanmar spans 92.2°E to 101.2°E, across UTM zones 46N (90°E to 96°E) and 47N (96°E to 102°E). Zone 47N is used for the whole country because its central meridian, 99°E, is at most 6.8° from any part of Myanmar, against 8.2° for the central meridian of zone 46N, 93°E: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-home_Ex02_files/figure-html/utm-zones-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: The population file before `select()` has 330 rows and 70 columns. The timeline below marks the coup (1 February 2021) and the start of Operation 1027 (27 October 2023): - **Military coup, 1 February 2021:** the military removed the elected government (@sec-intro; Wikipedia, "Myanmar conflict"). Armed conflict was already recorded in the ethnic states before the coup. The first quarter of the study period has one month before the coup and two after it. - **Operation 1027, 27 October 2023:** a coordinated offensive by "a coalition of three ethnic armed groups in Shan State", the Three Brotherhood Alliance of the Arakan Army, the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army and the Ta'ang National Liberation Army, "named Operation 1027, for the date the offensive commenced" (Council on Foreign Relations, 2026; date from Su Mon, 2024). The Council on Foreign Relations describes it as "the strongest challenge to military rule since the February 2021 coup". - **Use in the analysis:** the study period is divided at 27 October 2023 into the two phases compared in @sec-phases (RQ4). The charts of events and Gi\* over time mark it with a dashed line. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-home_Ex02_files/figure-html/study-timeline-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: # Data preparation and quality assessment {#sec-prep} ## Armed conflict events {#sec-event-types} ACLED codes six event types under three disorder types. The objectives are about violence, so the analysis variable includes only battles, explosions and remote violence, and violence against civilians. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-home_Ex02_files/figure-html/event-tree-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: callout-note ## ACLED event types The definitions are from the ACLED Codebook (ACLED, 2023, pp. 11 to 21). | Event type | What ACLED records | Used here | |--------------------|----------------------------------------------|--------| | Battles | Violent interaction between two organised armed groups | yes | | Explosions/Remote violence | Violence by bombs, shelling, airstrikes, drones or landmines, where the target cannot respond | yes | | Violence against civilians | Violence by an organised armed group against unarmed people | yes | | Protests | Public demonstration, mostly non-violent | no | | Riots | Violent demonstration, often unorganised | no | | Strategic developments | Non-violent events such as troop movements, arrests, agreements and territory transfers | no | Riots and protests count as demonstrations. The 285 riots and protests that ACLED codes under political violence are excluded, because ACLED classes these events as demonstrations. ::: ::: {.panel-tabset} #### Table ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} |event_type | events| fatalities| % of events| % of fatalities| |:--------------------------|------:|----------:|-----------:|---------------:| |Battles | 21,121| 59,287| 39.1| 66.4| |Explosions/Remote violence | 22,925| 20,735| 42.5| 23.2| |Violence against civilians | 9,958| 9,205| 18.4| 10.3| ::: ::: #### Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} armed_types <- c("Battles", "Explosions/Remote violence", "Violence against civilians") armed <- acled |> filter(event_type %in% armed_types) armed |> group_by(event_type) |> summarise(events = n(), fatalities = sum(fatalities)) |> mutate(`% of events` = 100 * events / sum(events), `% of fatalities` = 100 * fatalities / sum(fatalities)) |> kable(digits = 1, format.args = list(big.mark = ",")) ``` ::: ::: The three armed event types contain 54,004 events and 89,227 reported fatalities. Battles are 39% of the armed events and 66% of the fatalities. ## Assignment of events to townships {#sec-placement} Each event is assigned to a township by a point-in-polygon join on its latitude and longitude, after the points are projected to UTM zone 47N, the projection of the township layer. In the invented example below, points 1 and 2 are inside township A, point 3 is inside township B, and point 4 is outside townships A and B. `st_join()` returns one row for each point, with the `TS_PCODE` of the polygon that contains the point, and `NA` for point 4. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-home_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: The table below lists one event, at Muse (MMR10920), after each step. The test has five data requirements (slides 41 to 43 of the Lesson 5 deck): | Requirement | Source | In this report | |------------------------|-----------------------------------------|-------------------------------------| | No seasonal cycle | Slide 43; Hirsch et al. (1982) | Tested before the bin is chosen: not seasonal under the overall test | | No covariates | Slide 43; Helsel et al. (2020, p. 336) | No covariate is measured by township and quarter | | One value per period | Slide 43; Helsel et al. (2020, p. 344) | One count per township per quarter (@sec-cube) | | At least 8 to 10 periods | Slide 42; Kim and Lee (2023) | 19 quarters | | No serial correlation | Slide 41; Hamed and Rao (1998) | Not met: most Gi\* series are autocorrelated; corrected test run as a check (@sec-serial) | - **Seasonal cycle:** the test compares every quarter with every later quarter. A comparison across seasons "is really not informative about trend and is more likely to be an expression of the differences between seasons" (Helsel et al., 2020, p. 343). Seasonal variation "must be compensated for or removed", or "there may be only little power to detect trends which are truly present" (p. 342). The Seasonal Kendall test of Hirsch et al. (1982) compares each season only with the same season in other years. - **Covariates:** variables other than time, such as rainfall, "often have considerable influence" on a series (Helsel et al., 2020, p. 336). Removing their effect reduces the noise and increases the power of the test (p. 336). Population, the only township covariate in this report, is a single 2023 value per township (@sec-count-rate), constant across the 19 quarters. The Gi\* series are therefore tested without adjustment. - **Serial correlation:** the emerging hot spot classes on slides 44 and 45 are the classes of the ArcGIS emerging hot spot tool. The tool evaluates the trends "using the Mann-Kendall trend test", and its documentation describes no correction for serial correlation (Esri, n.d.). `emerging_hotspot_analysis()` and In-class Exercise 6 use the same uncorrected test. So do the two provided papers that use the ArcGIS tool (Kim and Lee, 2023; Boschan and Roman, 2024). The classes in this report use the uncorrected test, which keeps them identical to the definitions on slides 44 and 45. The correction of Hamed and Rao (1998) is applied as a check (@sec-serial). The ACLED events are recorded by day and have to be aggregated to a time bin. The provided papers use these bins: | Bin | Papers | |------------|------------------------------------------------------------------| | Year | Boschan and Roman (2024); Kim and Lee (2023); Mack and Kam (2018) | | 6 months | Kim and Lee (2023), for wild boar | | Month | Tan and Kam (2019) | | 5 days | Putrenko et al. (2018) | - **No seasonality test:** no provided paper reports a test for seasonality before choosing the bin. - **Minimum number of periods:** Kim and Lee (2023) use 6-month bins for wild boar because the ArcGIS space-time cube requires at least 10 time periods, close to the 8 to 10 time periods recommended on slide 42. - **Hidden patterns:** Boschan and Roman (2024) suggest that their annual bins may have hidden diminishing hot spots. - **Annual bins:** annual bins would give five periods, fewer than the 8 to 10 periods on slide 42. The last period would be nine months long. The candidates are months (57 periods) and quarters (19 periods). Ollech and Webel (2020, p. 27) describe this test as their next step after their comparison of seasonality tests. The test combines three p-values, and a series is seasonal if any of these holds: - the QS test on the residuals of a non-seasonal ARIMA model is below 0.01; - the Kruskal-Wallis test on the same residuals is below 0.001; - the QS test on the differenced series and the Kruskal-Wallis test on the residuals are both below 0.01. ::: {.panel-tabset} #### Table ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} |series | QS p, differenced| QS p, residuals| Kruskal-Wallis p, residuals|seasonal? | Friedman p (check)| |:---------------------|-----------------:|---------------:|---------------------------:|:---------|------------------:| |monthly, 57 periods | 0.468| 0.471| 0.357|FALSE | 0.219| |quarterly, 19 periods | 0.893| 1.000| 0.252|FALSE | 0.044| ::: ::: #### Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ts_m <- ts(monthly$n, start = c(2021, 1), frequency = 12) ts_q <- ts(quarterly$n, start = c(2021, 1), frequency = 4) wo <- map(list(ts_m, ts_q), combined_test) tibble(series = c("monthly, 57 periods", "quarterly, 19 periods"), `QS p, differenced` = map_dbl(wo, \(w) w$Pval[["QS p-value"]]), `QS p, residuals` = map_dbl(wo, \(w) w$Pval[["QS-R p-value"]]), `Kruskal-Wallis p, residuals` = map_dbl(wo, \(w) w$Pval[["KW-R p-value"]]), `seasonal?` = c(isSeasonal(ts_m), isSeasonal(ts_q)), `Friedman p (check)` = c(fried(ts_m)$Pval, fried(ts_q)$Pval)) |> kable(digits = 3) oct_dec <- fmt(round(mean(monthly$n[month(monthly$month) %in% 10:12]))) other_m <- fmt(round(mean(monthly$n[!month(monthly$month) %in% 10:12]))) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"} `ts()` turns the counts into series with 12 or 4 periods a year. `combined_test()` returns the three p-values of the overall test, `isSeasonal()` its decision, and `fried()` the Friedman check. ::: ::: ::: callout-note ## Seasonality tests: QS, Kruskal-Wallis and Friedman Each test checks whether the values in the same month (or quarter) of different years resemble each other more closely than is expected by chance. - The **QS test** checks the correlation between a value and the value 12 months earlier (4 quarters earlier for the quarterly series). A seasonal series repeats its pattern, so that correlation is positive and large. - The **Kruskal-Wallis** and **Friedman** tests rank the observations and compare the ranks of the 12 months (or 4 quarters). For example, if events are below the annual mean every January and above it every November, the ranks differ by month. - Both kinds of test need the trend removed first, so that a rising series does not look seasonal. The tests are run on the first differences of the series, the change from one period to the next, or on the residuals of an ARIMA model fitted without a seasonal term. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-home_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: The overall test classifies the monthly and the quarterly series as non-seasonal. The Friedman test is also run as a check. Ollech and Webel (2020, p. 26) identify "the modified QS and Friedman tests as the most informative seasonality tests" of the tests they compare. According to them, "the Friedman test mainly covers stable seasonality", while the QS test also covers seasonal patterns that change over time (p. 25). - **Monthly series:** the Friedman p-value is above 0.05, so no test finds seasonality. - **Quarterly series:** the Friedman p-value is below 0.05, weak evidence of seasonality. The quarters from October to December have the most events: 1,096 armed events per month, against 906 in the other months. ::: {.cell} ::: The main analysis uses quarterly bins: - **Seasonality:** the quarterly series is non-seasonal under the overall test. The weak seasonality that the Friedman test finds is checked with monthly bins (last item). - **Periods:** 19 quarters are above the 10-period minimum that Kim and Lee (2023) cite. - **Empty cells:** with quarterly bins, 31% of the cells of the cube have no armed event. With monthly bins, the share is 51%. - **Check with monthly bins:** emerging hot spot analysis is repeated with monthly bins (@sec-ehsa-sensitivity). No test finds seasonality in the monthly series. The monthly results show whether the classes change with the weak quarterly seasonality. They also show whether a longer bin hides diminishing hot spots, as Boschan and Roman (2024) suggest for their annual bins. ## Spatial weights: neighbours and the island problem {#sec-weights} ### Contiguity on Myanmar's coastline Under Queen contiguity, two townships are neighbours when they share any part of a boundary. Queen contiguity is the definition used in Hands-on Exercise 5 and in the provided papers that use contiguity (Stankov et al., 2017; Arif and Purnomo, 2017; Fergen and Bergstrom, 2021). ::: callout-note ## Contiguity: neighbours whose borders touch Under contiguity, two townships are neighbours when their borders touch. Distance plays no part. In the invented grid below, Rook contiguity counts a square as a neighbour only when the two squares share an edge, and Queen contiguity also counts a shared corner: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-home_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset} #### Output ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Min. 1st Qu. The 3 townships with no Queen neighbour also have no Rook neighbour. Three townships have no Queen neighbour: Chaungzon, Munaung and Cocokyun, all islands. The three islands and the mainland are four connected components of the neighbour graph. A township with no neighbours has no local statistic, so the three islands would not be assigned to any cluster: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-home_Ex02_files/figure-html/islands-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: callout-note ## Townships without neighbours: no local statistic A local statistic compares a township with the weighted average of its neighbours' values, the spatial lag. An island has no neighbours, so there is no average to compare with: - **By default, R stops.** `st_weights(nb_queen, style = "W")` fails with the error "Empty neighbour sets found (zero.policy: FALSE)". - **If empty neighbour sets are allowed** (`allow_zero = TRUE`), the spatial lag of an island is set to 0. Local Moran's I is then 0 and so is its variance, and the z-score, 0 divided by 0, is undefined (`NaN`). The class label is still computed, from the count and the lag of 0: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} |township | armed events| spatial lag| local I| variance of I| z-score|median label | |:---------|------------:|-----------:|-------:|-------------:|-------:|:------------| |Chaungzon | 12| 0| 0| 0| NaN|Low-Low | |Munaung | 3| 0| 0| 0| NaN|Low-Low | |Cocokyun | 0| 0| 0| 0| NaN|Low-Low | ::: ::: Anselin (2020a) warns about this case: "By construction, the spatially lagged variable will be zero, which may suggest spurious correlations." All three islands would carry the label Low-Low with no test behind it. ::: Neighbours can also be defined by the distance between townships, which requires one point to represent each township. In the course chapters on spatial weights, that point is computed with `st_centroid()`. In the MIMU layer, 41 townships consist of more than one polygon part, up to 159 parts, and the centroid of such a township can lie outside it. ::: {.panel-tabset} #### Output ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Demoso" "Kawlin" "Kyaukse" "Rathedaung" "Kyaukpyu" [6] "Cocokyun" "Labutta" "Pyapon" ``` ::: ::: #### Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cen <- st_centroid(st_geometry(tsp)) pos <- st_point_on_surface(st_geometry(tsp)) outside <- !mapply(\(p, g) st_intersects(p, g, sparse = FALSE)[1, 1], cen, st_geometry(tsp)) tsp$TS[outside] ``` ::: ::: ::: callout-note ## Township points: centroid versus point on surface The centroid is the centre of mass of a shape. For a crescent, a ring of islands or a coastline with several offshore pieces, the centre of mass may lie in the sea or in the next township. A point on surface is a point chosen to lie inside the polygon of the township. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-home_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: For 8 townships, the centroid lies outside the township. Points on surface are used for every township-to-township distance in this report: - **Inside the township:** `st_point_on_surface()` "returns a point guaranteed to be on the (multi)surface" (Pebesma, 2026). The centroid has no such guarantee. - **The same points as sfdep:** when given polygons, the sfdep functions that measure distance, including `st_knn()`, `st_inverse_distance()`, `critical_threshold()` and `st_dist_band()`, replace them with `st_point_on_surface()` and print "Polygon provided. Using point on surface." (Parry, 2024). Computing the points once, as `pos`, keeps every distance in this report on the same points as these functions. ### Contiguity with three added links, and k-nearest neighbours In the provided papers, the island problem is handled with k-nearest neighbours: - **Mack and Kam (2018):** Rook and Queen contiguity left African regions without neighbours, Madagascar among them, so Mack and Kam moved to k-nearest neighbours with $k = 8$, the smallest $k$ they tested. - **Khan et al. (2017):** the authors use $k = 8$, the minimum number of neighbours in the ESRI documentation they cite. Under contiguity, the neighbours of a township are the townships that share a boundary with it. Fighting in Myanmar moves between adjacent townships along roads: Su Mon (2024) describes resistance groups blocking military reinforcements on the Mandalay-Lashio road. The main weights are Queen contiguity with one added link for each island: - **Source:** in the spdep guide "No-neighbour observation and subgraph handling", Bivand (2026) joins the island constituency of Ynys Môn, in Wales, to its nearest mainland neighbours. Linking each island separately "does not risk adding spurious neighbours in denser parts of the study area". - **Nearest township:** each island is linked to its nearest township, measured between points on surface. - **Both directions:** the link is added "by symmetry" (Bivand, 2026), because the nearest-neighbour relation "is not a symmetric relation" (Anselin, 2020a). - **Boundary distance:** Bivand (2026) measures the distance between polygon boundaries. Under boundary distance, Munaung and Cocokyun have the same nearest township. Chaungzon lies within 0.8 km of three townships across the river: Mudon (0.2 km), Paung and Mawlamyine (0.8 km each). - **Neighbour count:** Queen contiguity gives a mean of 5.2 neighbours per township, below the guideline of about eight neighbours for skewed counts on slide 39 of the Lesson 5 deck. ::: {.cell} ::: k-nearest neighbours are run as a check on the contiguity weights (@sec-weights-check): - **Unequal sizes:** according to slide 36 of the Lesson 5 deck, "the polygon contiguity method is effective when polygons are similar in size and distribution." The 90th percentile of township area is 81 times the 10th percentile. - **Rural areas:** Mack and Kam (2018, p. 7) chose their smallest weight matrix because counting second-order neighbours "presents a methodological problem for the larger, more rural areas" of Africa. - **Values of $k$:** $k = 8$ is on slide 39 of the Lesson 5 deck, in Mack and Kam (2018) and in Khan et al. (2017). $k = 6$ is close to the mean number of neighbours under Queen contiguity. ::: callout-note ## Contiguity and townships of unequal size Near places tend to be more alike than distant ones (Tobler, 1970), so a neighbour is meant to be a nearby township. Under contiguity, a neighbour is any township with a shared border, whatever the distance. In the MIMU layer, the distance to the neighbours varies with township size: | Township | Area | Queen neighbours | Median distance to the neighbours | |------------------------|--------------|------------|------------------| | Pabedan, Yangon (smallest) | 0.6 km² | 5 | 1.5 km | | Tanai, Kachin (largest) | 12,347 km² | 7 | 113 km | Distances are measured between points on surface. Under contiguity, the neighbours of the smallest and the largest township count equally, although those of Tanai are about 77 times farther away. The townships are not similar in size, the condition on slide 36 quoted above. k-nearest neighbours are also run for this reason (@sec-weights-check). The number of neighbours also varies, from 1 to 11. Row-standardised weights (`style = "W"`), the setting listed for contiguity on slide 36, give the neighbours of each township a total weight of 1. The Lesson 5 slides list the Getis-Ord Global G separately, under "Measures of Global High/Low Clustering" (slide 16). Global G tests whether pairs of high counts or pairs of low counts dominate the pairs of neighbours. In the Lesson 5 slides and in the four provided papers that map local statistics (Mack and Kam, 2018; Khan et al., 2017; Stankov et al., 2017; Arif and Purnomo, 2017), global Moran's I is run before the local statistics. No provided paper uses Global G. ::: callout-note ## Global Moran's I, Geary's C and Getis-Ord Global G Moran's I, Geary's C and Global G are each a sum of one term per pair of neighbouring townships, divided by a total for the whole map (Lesson 5 slides 9 to 12, 16 and 17): $$I = \frac{n}{W} \cdot \frac{\sum_i \sum_j w_{ij} (x_i - \bar{x})(x_j - \bar{x})}{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^2}$$ $$\text{Moran's } I = \frac{\text{townships}}{\text{sum of weights}} \cdot \frac{\sum \text{weight} \, (\text{count} - \text{mean}) (\text{neighbour} - \text{mean})} {\sum (\text{count} - \text{mean})^2}$$ $$C = \frac{n - 1}{2W} \cdot \frac{\sum_i \sum_j w_{ij} (x_i - x_j)^2}{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^2}$$ $$\text{Geary's } C = \frac{\text{townships} - 1}{2 \times \text{sum of weights}} \cdot \frac{\sum \text{weight} \times (\text{count} - \text{neighbour's count})^2} {\sum (\text{count} - \text{mean})^2}$$ $$G = \frac{\sum_i \sum_{j \neq i} w_{ij} \, x_i x_j}{\sum_i \sum_{j \neq i} x_i x_j}$$ $$\text{Global } G = \frac{\sum \text{weight} \times \text{count} \times \text{neighbour's count}} {\sum \text{count} \times \text{other township's count}}$$ where $x_i$ is the count of township $i$, $\bar{x}$ is the mean count, $w_{ij}$ is the weight of the pair $i$ and $j$ (0 when townships $i$ and $j$ are not neighbours), $n$ is the number of townships and $W$ is the sum of the weights. For example, a pair of neighbours with 9 events each contributes 16 to Moran's I, 0 to Geary's C and 81 to Global G: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-home_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-39-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: - **Moran's I and Geary's C:** a pair of low values counts the same as a pair of high values, so these two statistics measure whether similar values are neighbours. The expectation of Moran's I is −0.003 for 330 townships. - **Getis-Ord Global G:** a pair of 1 and 1 contributes 1 to Global G. Global G above its expectation indicates that high values are neighbours (slide 17). Global G below its expectation indicates that low values are neighbours, when pairs of low values "dominate" the map (Getis and Ord, 1992, p. 198). - **Moran's I with Global G:** Getis and Ord (1992, p. 198) recommend using Moran's I and Global G together. According to them, Moran's I does not "discriminate between patterns that have high values dominant within d or low values dominant", where $d$ is the distance band. The expectation of Global G is $\frac{W}{n(n - 1)}$, where $W$ is the sum of the weights and $n$ is the number of townships. The formula on slide 21 of the Lesson 5 deck divides by a slightly different variance, which changes the size of $I_i$ but not its sign, class or pseudo p-value; the formula here is the one `local_moran()` computes. With row-standardised weights, $\sum_j w_{ij} (x_j - \bar{x})$ is the neighbours' average minus the mean. In the Moran scatterplot, each township is plotted by its own count ($x$) and its neighbours' average ($y$), each as a deviation from the mean (Anselin, 1996). The four quadrants of the plot are the LISA classes. Anselin (1996) draws the dividing lines at the mean. It is also below the lowest neighbours' average of any significant High-High township, 333 events. ## Local Geary's c {#sec-local-geary} ::: callout-note ## Local Geary's c: squared differences and cluster labels Local Geary's c is the weighted sum of the squared differences between the standardised count of a township and those of its neighbours (Anselin, 2019): $$c_i = \sum_j w_{ij} (z_i - z_j)^2$$ $$\text{local } c = \sum \text{weight} \times (\text{standardised count} - \text{neighbour's standardised count})^2$$ where $z_i$ and $z_j$ are the counts of townships $i$ and $j$, each minus the mean and divided by the standard deviation. The formula on slide 27 of the Lesson 5 deck uses deviations from the mean; `local_c_perm()` also divides them by the standard deviation, which changes the size of $c_i$ but not its pseudo p-value. A small value means the township is similar to its neighbours; a large value means it differs from them. "Since there is no cross-product involved, there is no direct relation to linear similarity", so local Geary's c "may detect patterns that escape the Local Moran, and vice versa" (Anselin, 2020b). Slide 27 of the Lesson 5 deck lists local Geary's c under other forms of LISA. Anselin (2019) first separates a small c (a township similar to its neighbours) from a large c (a township different from its neighbours), then labels a small c by the township's count and its neighbours' average. The labels in this report are those of Anselin (2019), with the dividing lines at the median as for local Moran's I (@sec-lisa-labels): | Label | Meaning | |----------------|--------------------------------------------------------------| | High-High | c is below its expected value, and the township's count and its neighbours' average are above their medians | | Low-Low | c is below its expected value, and the township's count and its neighbours' average are at or below their medians | | Other Positive | c is below its expected value, and the township's count and its neighbours' average are on different sides of their medians | | Negative | c is above its expected value | ::: ::: {.panel-tabset} #### Table ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} |cluster | n| |:---------------|---:| |High-High | 45| |Low-Low | 57| |Other Positive | 6| |Negative | 4| |Not significant | 218| ::: ::: #### Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(2610) geary <- tsp |> mutate(local_c = local_c_perm(armed, nb, wt, nsim = 999), .before = 1) |> unnest(local_c) |> mutate(cluster = case_when(p_ci_sim >= 0.05 ~ "Not significant", ci > e_ci ~ "Negative", armed > median(armed) & lag_armed > median(lag_armed) ~ "High-High", armed <= median(armed) & lag_armed <= median(lag_armed) ~ "Low-Low", .default = "Other Positive"), cluster = factor(cluster, levels = c("High-High", "Low-Low", "Other Positive", "Negative", "Not significant"))) count(st_drop_geometry(geary), cluster) |> kable() ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"} `local_c_perm()` returns local $c$ (`ci`), its permutation mean (`e_ci`) and its pseudo p-value. The count is above its median and the neighbours' average is below its median in each of them. ## Getis-Ord Gi and Gi\* {#sec-gi} Getis and Ord (1992) define Gi\* as the weighted sum of the counts of a township and its neighbours, divided by the sum of all counts (Lesson 5 slide 30): $$G_i^* = \frac{\sum_j w_{ij} x_j}{\sum_j x_j}$$ $$\text{G}_i^* = \frac{\text{weighted sum of the counts of the township and its neighbours}} {\text{sum of all counts}}$$ `local_gstar_perm()` returns Gi\* as a z-score: the weighted sum minus the same sum at the mean count, divided by the standard deviation of that sum (Ord and Getis, 1995; Lesson 5 slide 31): $$Z(G_i^*) = \frac{\sum_j w_{ij} x_j - \bar{x} \sum_j w_{ij}} {S \sqrt{\left[ n \sum_j w_{ij}^2 - \left( \sum_j w_{ij} \right)^2 \right] / (n - 1)}}$$ $$Z(\text{G}_i^*) = \frac{\text{weighted sum of the counts} - \text{the same sum at the mean}} {\text{standard deviation of that sum}}$$ where $x_j$ is the count of township $j$, $\bar{x}$ is the mean count, $w_{ij}$ is the row-standardised weight, $n$ is the number of townships and $S$ is the standard deviation of the counts. The sums over $j$ include the township itself. Gi is the same statistic without the township's own count. ::: {.panel-tabset} #### Output ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Gi Gi* Hot spot Cold spot Not significant Hot spot 36 0 3 Cold spot 0 46 6 Not significant 0 4 235 ``` ::: ::: #### Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nb_self <- include_self(nb) wt_self <- st_weights(nb_self, style = "W") spot_of <- \(z, p) case_when(p >= 0.05 ~ "Not significant", z > 0 ~ "Hot spot", .default = "Cold spot") set.seed(2610) gistar <- tsp |> mutate(g = local_gstar_perm(armed, nb_self, wt_self, nsim = 999), .before = 1) |> unnest(g) |> mutate(spot = factor(spot_of(gi_star, p_sim), c("Hot spot", "Cold spot", "Not significant"))) set.seed(2610) gi <- tsp |> mutate(g = local_g_perm(armed, nb, wt, nsim = 999), .before = 1) |> unnest(g) |> mutate(spot = factor(spot_of(gi, p_sim), c("Hot spot", "Cold spot", "Not significant"))) table(`Gi*` = gistar$spot, Gi = gi$spot) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"} `include_self()` adds each township to its own neighbour list, which turns Gi into Gi\*. `local_gstar_perm()` and `local_g_perm()` return the z-score and the pseudo p-value, and `spot_of()` labels hot and cold spots by the sign of the z-score where p < 0.05 (Getis and Ord, 1992). Mack and Kam (2018, p. 7) find that "the increase in the number of neighbors have the effect of smoothening out the Moran's I scores", with the highest Moran's I at $k = 8$ and the lowest at $k = 28$. Global Moran's I is computed here under Queen contiguity and under k-nearest neighbours with $k = 6$ and $k = 8$. ::: {.cell} ::: ::: callout-note ## Spatial lags under a high $k$: the smoothing effect Each township's spatial lag is the average count of its $k$ nearest townships. A later value above the earlier one scores +1, a later value below scores -1, and a tie scores 0 (Helsel et al., 2020, p. 217). The sum of these scores is $S$. Kendall's $\tau$ is $S$ divided by the number of pairs of quarters: $$S = \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} \sum_{j=k+1}^{n} \operatorname{sgn}(x_j - x_k), \quad \tau = \frac{S}{n(n - 1)/2}$$ $$S = \text{pairs with a rise} - \text{pairs with a fall}, \quad \tau = \frac{S}{\text{pairs of quarters}}$$ where $x_k$ and $x_j$ are the values in quarters $k$ and $j$, and $n$ is the number of quarters. The formula of $\tau$ is for a series without ties; `MannKendall()` adjusts $\tau$ for tied values. $\tau$ ranges from $-1$ for a series that falls at every step to $+1$ for a series that rises at every step. The null hypothesis is no monotonic trend. Only the direction of each change enters the sum, so $\tau$ is unchanged if every count is replaced by its rank. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} | | | | | | | | For the Gi\* series of one township, $x_1, \dots, x_{19}$: $$r_1 = \frac{\sum_{t=2}^{19} (x_t - \bar{x})(x_{t-1} - \bar{x})} {\sum_{t=1}^{19} (x_t - \bar{x})^2}$$ $$r_1 = \frac{\sum (\text{quarter} - \text{mean}) \times (\text{previous quarter} - \text{mean})} {\sum (\text{quarter} - \text{mean})^2}$$ where $\bar{x}$ is the mean of the 19 values. A value near 0 means that the Gi\* of one quarter is unrelated to the Gi\* of the next quarter. A value near 1 means that high quarters follow high quarters and low quarters follow low quarters. For 19 independent values, $r_1$ lies within $\pm 1.96/\sqrt{19} = \pm 0.45$ in about 95% of series, the bound drawn on an `acf()` plot in R. A value above 0.45 is therefore significant at the 5% level. Example: six quarters with the values 1, 2, 4, 5, 4 and 2 have a mean of 3. Each quarter's deviation from the mean is multiplied by the deviation of the quarter before it: | Quarter | $x_t - \bar{x}$ | $x_{t-1} - \bar{x}$ | Product | |---------|-----------------|---------------------|---------| | 2 | −1 | −2 | 2 | | 3 | 1 | −1 | −1 | | 4 | 2 | 1 | 2 | | 5 | 1 | 2 | 2 | | 6 | −1 | 1 | −1 | The products sum to 4 and the squared deviations to $4 + 1 + 1 + 4 + 1 + 1 = 12$, so $r_1 = 4/12 = 0.33$. Most products are positive because low quarters follow low quarters and high quarters follow high quarters. Minbya (MMR012005) has the median $r_1$ of the 330 townships, 0.65. Its Gi\* is below −1 in every quarter from 2021 Q2 to 2022 Q2 and above 3 in 2024 Q1 and Q2. The Mann-Kendall variance of Hamed and Rao (1998) is larger for a series with positive autocorrelation. ::: The lag-1 autocorrelation of the Gi\* series has a median of 0.65. The lag-1 autocorrelation is above 0.45, the 5% critical value for 19 quarters, in 255 of the 330 townships (77%). Some of this correlation arises from the time lag in Gi\*: with `k = 1`, the Gi\* of a quarter includes the neighbours' values from the previous quarter (@sec-ehsa-classes). ::: {.cell} ::: The classes in @sec-ehsa-classes use the uncorrected test (@sec-bin). callout-note ## Cohen's kappa: agreement beyond chance The share of townships in the same class before and after 27 October 2023 is inflated by the townships that are not significant in either phase, which are in the same class by chance. Of the 330 townships, 203 are not significant in either phase. Cohen's kappa (Cohen, 1960) removes the agreement expected by chance: $$\kappa = \frac{p_o - p_e}{1 - p_e}$$ $$\kappa = \frac{\text{observed agreement} - \text{agreement expected by chance}} {1 - \text{agreement expected by chance}}$$ where $p_o$ is the share of townships in the same class in both phases, and $p_e$ is the share expected if the classes of the two phases were independent: for each class, the share of townships in that class before 27 October 2023 multiplied by the share after it, summed over the classes. A kappa of 1 means identical classes, and a kappa of 0 means agreement equal to chance. A kappa of 0.45, for example, means that the observed agreement covers 45% of the gap between chance agreement and identical classes. Boschan and Roman (2024, Table 3) compare hot spot maps of two periods with a spatial fuzzy version of the statistic, which "captures the strength of the statistical relationship that underlies the comparison, somewhat like the use of a correlation coefficient" (p. 6). ::: ::: {.cell} ::: The number of armed events per month rose from 854 before 27 October 2023 to 1,080 after it. Fergen and Bergstrom (2021) use bivariate LISA to ask whether one variable in a county is associated with another variable in the neighbouring counties. Here bivariate local Moran's I tests whether violence against civilians in a township is associated with battles in the neighbouring townships. ::: callout-note ## Bivariate local Moran's I The bivariate statistic is the product of the township's standardised count of violence against civilians and the average standardised count of battles in its neighbours: $$I_i^B = z_{v,i} \sum_j w_{ij} \, z_{b,j}$$ $$\text{bivariate } I = \text{violence } z \times \text{neighbours' average battle } z$$ where $z_{v,i}$ is the standardised count of violence against civilians in township $i$, $z_{b,j}$ is the standardised count of battles in township $j$, and $w_{ij}$ is the row-standardised weight. Up to a constant, $I_i^B$ is the term of township $i$ in the sum on slide 28. A township is High-High when its count of violence against civilians and its neighbours' average battle count are both above their medians, and High-Low when the first is above its median and the second below. Fewer events may be recorded than occurred in areas closed to observers, so some cold spots may be gaps in reporting. Four of the eight townships with no recorded event are in districts governed by the United Wa State Army (@sec-prep), where reporting may be limited. - **Population.** A township with more people may have more armed events. Townships with high rates per 100,000 people are also neighbours of each other: Moran's I of the log rate is 0.67 (@sec-count-rate). Population size may therefore explain only part of the clustering of the counts. - **Location precision.** Geo-precision 2 events are placed at a nearby town. The clusters of township counts may depend in part on the locations of those towns. Geo-precision 2 events are 45% of the events analysed (@sec-precision), so an effect of location precision cannot be excluded. # Implications for peace-building {#sec-implications} ::: {.cell} ::: The maps describe where armed conflict has been recorded. ACLED records reported events, so the implications below concern where events are recorded, and not their causes or the needs of the population. The townships named below are labelled on the maps of @sec-bivariate and @sec-ehsa-classes. - **Violence against civilians next to battles:** in the High-High townships of the bivariate map (@sec-bivariate), in the central dry zone, Tanintharyi, Kayin and northern Shan, violence against civilians and battles are both recorded in neighbouring townships. Su Mon (2024) describes the military turning "to the closest civilian population center to detain, torture, and kill" after losses, and rivalry between resistance groups that "can impede the delivery of humanitarian aid". Protection of civilians and humanitarian access may be priorities in these townships. - **Violence against civilians next to few battles:** in the 15 High-Low townships of Yangon, violence against civilians is above the median and the battle counts of the neighbours are below it. Su Mon (2024) describes resistance groups that "opportunistically assassinate military-appointed administrators" and civilians "detained by the military or resistance groups under the impression of being informants". Monitoring of detentions and targeted killings may be relevant in these townships. - **Hot quarters at the end of the period:** Kim and Lee (2023, p. 8) give priority to "persistent hotspots or intensifying hotspots" of wildlife-vehicle collisions on expressways. In this report, no township is in either class. The consecutive and oscillating hot spots, around Mandalay and in Nawnghkio in northern Shan (@sec-ehsa-classes), are hot in the last quarters of the period, so they may be the first places for monitoring. - **Cold spots:** a cold spot has few recorded events, which may come from little fighting or from little reporting. Three of the 13 persistent cold spots before the filter are in Matman District, which the United Wa State Army has governed since its ceasefire of May 1989 (@sec-prep). Verification of reporting in these townships may be needed before they are treated as quiet. # Limitations {#sec-limitations} | Limitation | Effect on the results | |--------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------| | Reported events only | Cold spots and zero counts may partly reflect limited access for reporters | | Equal weight per event | A skirmish and an airstrike count the same.
